meta.note: Original CISSP-style practice questions. matching questions carry a prompts[] (left items numbered 1..n) and options[] (right items A..n); correct_answer encodes the pairing. sequence_ordering correct_answer lists option labels in correct order.

questions.question: Which statement BEST distinguishes a security audit from a security test?

options.label: A
options.text: A test is performed only by external regulators

options.label: B
options.text: A test always checks compliance while an audit attacks the system

options.label: C
options.text: An audit focuses on verifying compliance with governance/regulations and reporting on posture; a test exercises a control to see if it works

options.label: D
options.text: An audit and a test are identical activities

explanation.why_correct: A security audit evaluates compliance with governance, regulations, and overall security posture (reporting status and risk impact); a test exercises specific controls to verify they function.

why_others_are_wrong.B: This reverses the roles—audits emphasize compliance verification.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Audits and tests serve different purposes.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Tests can be performed internally or by hired testers, not only regulators.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes compliance-focused audits from control-exercising tests.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 6 > Security Test and Assessment > Security Test and Assessment Overview

questions.question: An internal security audit is characterized by being:

options.label: A
options.text: Performed by an outside firm and reported to regulators only

options.label: B
options.text: Prohibited before an external audit

options.label: C
options.text: Performed by internal personnel and reported to senior management

options.label: D
options.text: Always more objective than an external audit

explanation.why_correct: Internal audits are conducted by internal staff and reported to senior management, often as a self-audit before an external audit.

why_others_are_wrong.A: That describes an external/third-party audit.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Internal audits are generally LESS objective than independent external audits.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Internal self-audits are commonly performed before external audits.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of the internal audit definition.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 6 > Security Test and Assessment > Types of Security Audits

questions.question: A business partner hires an outside firm to audit a vendor and have the results reported back to the partner (not the vendor) for an acquisition decision. This is BEST described as a:

options.label: A
options.text: Internal audit

options.label: B
options.text: Penetration test

options.label: C
options.text: Third-party audit

options.label: D
options.text: Self-assessment

explanation.why_correct: A third-party audit is performed by an outside team on behalf of another organization, with results reported to that organization—common for compliance or acquisition due diligence.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Internal audits are run by the audited org's own staff and report to its management.
why_others_are_wrong.D: A self-assessment is performed by the org on itself.
why_others_are_wrong.B: A penetration test simulates attacks, not a compliance audit reported to a third party.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps an outside-org-directed audit to a third-party audit.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 6 > Security Test and Assessment > Types of Security Audits

questions.question: The PRIMARY value of an external audit (conducted by an outside specialist firm) is that it:

options.label: A
options.text: Is always cheaper than an internal audit

options.label: B
options.text: Requires no scope definition

options.label: C
options.text: Provides an unbiased, independent perspective

options.label: D
options.text: Eliminates the need for any internal controls

explanation.why_correct: External audits provide an independent, unbiased perspective, reporting to executive officers.

why_others_are_wrong.A: External audits are often more costly, not cheaper.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Scope must still be defined for any audit.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Audits assess controls; they do not remove the need for them.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the independence value of external audits.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 6 > Security Test and Assessment > Types of Security Audits

questions.question: A Key Risk Indicator (KRI) differs from a Key Performance Indicator (KPI) in that a KRI:

options.label: A
options.text: Measures only past financial profit

options.label: B
options.text: Measures potential failure or ineffectiveness in security controls (forward-looking risk)

options.label: C
options.text: Can only be expressed as a color code

options.label: D
options.text: Is identical to a KPI in every way

explanation.why_correct: A KRI measures the potential for failure/ineffectiveness of controls—signaling rising risk—whereas a KPI measures performance against objectives.

why_others_are_wrong.A: KRIs concern security-control risk, not just financial profit.
why_others_are_wrong.D: KRIs and KPIs measure different things (risk vs performance).
why_others_are_wrong.C: KRIs are not limited to color codes.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes KRIs (risk) from KPIs (performance).

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 6 > Security Test and Assessment > Key Risk Indicators (KRIs)

questions.question: A Key Performance Indicator (KPI) in security assessment is BEST used to:

options.label: A
options.text: Define the office floor plan

options.label: B
options.text: Predict the exact date of the next breach

options.label: C
options.text: Measure how well security activities are meeting defined objectives/targets

options.label: D
options.text: Replace all logging and monitoring

explanation.why_correct: KPIs measure performance against goals/targets (e.g., percentage of systems patched on time), helping gauge program effectiveness.

why_others_are_wrong.B: KPIs measure performance, not predict exact breach dates.
why_others_are_wrong.D: KPIs complement, not replace, monitoring.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Floor plans are unrelated to KPIs.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the performance-measurement role of KPIs.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 6 > Security Test and Assessment > Performance and Risk Indicators

questions.question: Which pair of standards provides guidance on security measurement and metrics?

options.label: A
options.text: PCI DSS and HIPAA

options.label: B
options.text: NIST SP 800-88 and ISO 11889

options.label: C
options.text: WPA2 and WPA3

options.label: D
options.text: NIST SP 800-55 and ISO 27004

explanation.why_correct: NIST SP 800-55 and ISO 27004 both address security measurement, metrics, and evaluation.

why_others_are_wrong.B: NIST SP 800-88 is media sanitization; ISO 11889 is TPM.
why_others_are_wrong.A: PCI DSS/HIPAA are compliance regulations, not measurement guides.
why_others_are_wrong.C: WPA2/WPA3 are wireless encryption protocols.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps security metrics guidance to NIST 800-55/ISO 27004.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 6 > Security Test and Assessment > Measurement Standards and Guides

questions.question: A team must collect assessment data but has limited time and budget. The guide frames this trade-off using the triple constraint of:

options.label: A
options.text: Confidentiality, integrity, and availability

options.label: B
options.text: Red, blue, and purple teams

options.label: C
options.text: People, process, and technology

options.label: D
options.text: Scope, time, and cost (which together affect data quality)

explanation.why_correct: The triple constraint of scope, time, and cost governs the quality of collected assessment data—expanding one usually pressures the others.

why_others_are_wrong.C: People/process/technology is a different model, not the triple constraint here.
why_others_are_wrong.A: CIA is the security triad, not the project triple constraint.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Red/blue/purple are testing teams, not constraints.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps the scope/time/cost trade-off to the triple constraint.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 6 > Security Test and Assessment > Collecting Security Data

questions.question: Reviewing account management data during an assessment primarily helps verify that:

options.label: A
options.text: The data center temperature is correct

options.label: B
options.text: The office has enough parking

options.label: C
options.text: The wireless encryption is WPA3

options.label: D
options.text: Account creation, modification, and removal follow policy (e.g., no orphaned or excessive accounts)

explanation.why_correct: Account management data (identities and authenticators across the account lifecycle) lets assessors verify proper creation, modification, and auditing of accounts—catching orphaned or over-privileged accounts.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Temperature is an environmental control concern.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Wireless encryption is a network control, not account data.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Parking is unrelated to account management.

questions.exam_reasoning: Connects account management data to lifecycle verification.

options.label: C

options.label: D
options.text: Permission from external attackers

explanation.why_correct: Assessments require management approval and support to authorize scope, access, and resources.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Furniture is irrelevant to assessment authorization.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Attackers do not authorize assessments.
why_others_are_wrong.C: A UPS is a power device, not assessment authorization.

questions.question: Order the disaster recovery test types from LEAST disruptive/intensive to MOST disruptive. (Provide the option labels in order.)

options.label: A
options.text: Checklist (read-through) test

options.label: B
options.text: Parallel test

options.label: C
options.text: Structured walkthrough (tabletop)

options.label: D
options.text: Full interruption test

options.label: E
options.text: Simulation test

explanation.why_correct: DR tests escalate from a checklist review, to a tabletop walkthrough, to a simulation, to a parallel test (no impact to live ops), to a full interruption test (production is impacted).

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the order of DR test intensity.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 6 > Security Test and Assessment > Disaster Recovery Test Types and Considerations

questions.question: A company wants to validate that its recovery site can run production workloads WITHOUT taking the live production environment offline. Which DR test fits BEST?

options.label: A
options.text: Checklist (read-through) test

options.label: B
options.text: Structured walkthrough (tabletop)

options.label: C
options.text: Parallel test

options.label: D
options.text: Full interruption test

explanation.why_correct: A parallel test runs recovery procedures/site in parallel without impacting live operations—validating recovery capability with low risk.

why_others_are_wrong.D: A full interruption test deliberately impacts production, which the requirement forbids.
why_others_are_wrong.A: A checklist test only reviews documents, not actual recovery operations.
why_others_are_wrong.B: A tabletop exercise discusses the plan but does not run the recovery site.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps no-impact recovery validation to a parallel test.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 6 > Security Test and Assessment > Disaster Recovery Test Types and Considerations

questions.question: Which DR test is the MOST thorough but also the RISKIEST, because production operations are actually moved to the backup site?

options.label: A
options.text: Checklist test

options.label: B
options.text: Full interruption test

options.label: C
options.text: Parallel test

options.label: D
options.text: Simulation test

explanation.why_correct: A full interruption test moves production to the backup site, impacting live operations—most realistic and thorough but highest risk.

why_others_are_wrong.C: A parallel test does not impact live operations.
why_others_are_wrong.D: A simulation walks through a scenario without full production cutover.
why_others_are_wrong.A: A checklist test only reviews documentation.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps highest-risk production cutover to the full interruption test.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 6 > Security Test and Assessment > Disaster Recovery Test Types and Considerations

questions.question: A structured walkthrough (tabletop) DR test consists of:

options.label: A
options.text: Team members reviewing the DR plan together in a meeting to identify issues

options.label: B
options.text: Sending invalid data to an application to find bugs

options.label: C
options.text: Scanning the network for open ports

options.label: D
options.text: Actually failing over production to a cloud site

explanation.why_correct: A structured walkthrough/tabletop exercise gathers the team to review the DR plan and identify gaps—discussion-based, no live failover.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Failing over production is a full interruption test.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Sending invalid data is fuzz testing.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Port scanning is a vulnerability-scanning activity.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of the tabletop/structured walkthrough test.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 6 > Security Test and Assessment > Disaster Recovery Test Types and Considerations

questions.question: A differential backup copies:

options.label: A
options.text: The entire system every time

options.label: B
options.text: Nothing; it only verifies existing backups

options.label: C
options.text: Only data modified since the last full OR incremental backup

options.label: D
options.text: All data modified since the last FULL backup

explanation.why_correct: A differential backup copies everything changed since the last full backup (so differentials grow until the next full backup).

why_others_are_wrong.C: Copying changes since the last full OR incremental describes an incremental backup.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Backing up everything each time describes a full backup.
why_others_are_wrong.B: A differential backup copies changed data; it is not merely a verification.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes differential (since last full) from incremental.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 6 > Security Test and Assessment > Backup Types and Testing Requirements

questions.question: An organization runs a full backup on Sunday and incremental backups each weeknight. To FULLY restore data after a Thursday failure, which sets are needed?

options.label: A
options.text: Any single incremental backup

options.label: B
options.text: Only Thursday's incremental backup

options.label: C
options.text: The Sunday full backup plus every incremental from Monday through Thursday

options.label: D
options.text: Only the Sunday full backup

explanation.why_correct: Incrementals capture only changes since the last full or incremental, so a full restore needs the full backup plus the complete chain of incrementals up to the failure.

why_others_are_wrong.B: A single incremental lacks all prior changes since the full backup.
why_others_are_wrong.D: The full backup alone misses changes made during the week.
why_others_are_wrong.A: One incremental is insufficient; the entire chain is required.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests incremental restore requiring full + full incremental chain.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 6 > Security Test and Assessment > Backup Types and Testing Requirements

questions.question: A full backup is:

options.label: A
options.text: A scan for open network ports

options.label: B
options.text: A copy of only the files changed since yesterday

options.label: C
options.text: A complete copy of all system and user data

options.label: D
options.text: A read-through review of the backup plan

explanation.why_correct: A full backup captures a complete copy of all objects and user data, enabling a complete restore from one set.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Copying only recent changes describes incremental/differential backups.
why_others_are_wrong.D: A read-through review is a checklist DR test.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Port scanning is a vulnerability-assessment activity.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of the full backup definition.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 6 > Security Test and Assessment > Backup Types and Testing Requirements

questions.question: During a security assessment, the MOST important thing to verify about backups is that they:

options.label: A
options.text: Can actually be restored, and are retained/encrypted/archived per policy

options.label: B
options.text: Are never tested to avoid wear

options.label: C
options.text: Use the brightest-colored tapes

options.label: D
options.text: Are stored on the same server as production data

explanation.why_correct: Backups must be tested for successful restoration and verified for retention, encryption, and proper archiving—an untested backup is unreliable.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Storing backups with production defeats their disaster-recovery purpose.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Backups must be tested; untested backups may fail when needed.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Tape color is irrelevant to backup integrity.

questions.exam_reasoning: Emphasizes restore-testing and proper backup handling.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 6 > Security Test and Assessment > Backup Data Testing and Verification

questions.question: Collecting security training and awareness data during an assessment helps the organization:

options.label: A
options.text: Eliminate the need for any technical controls

options.label: B
options.text: Guarantee no employee will ever click a phishing link

options.label: C
options.text: Replace the disaster recovery plan

options.label: D
options.text: Track compliance with training requirements and identify gaps for emerging risks

explanation.why_correct: Training/awareness data verifies who has completed required training, tracks compliance, and reveals gaps relative to emerging risks.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Training complements, not replaces, technical controls.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Training reduces but cannot guarantee zero risky behavior.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Training data does not replace DR planning.

questions.exam_reasoning: Connects training data to compliance tracking and gap analysis.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 6 > Security Test and Assessment > Verifying Training and Awareness

questions.question: A checklist (read-through) DR test involves:

options.label: A
options.text: Distributing the DR checklist to team members to review and provide feedback

options.label: B
options.text: Exploiting vulnerabilities with Metasploit

options.label: C
options.text: Cutting over production to the backup site

options.label: D
options.text: Encrypting all backup tapes

explanation.why_correct: A checklist/read-through test distributes the DR plan/checklist for review and feedback—the least disruptive DR test.

why_others_are_wrong.C: Production cutover is a full interruption test.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Exploitation with Metasploit is a penetration-testing activity.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Encrypting tapes is a backup-handling control, not a DR test type.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of the checklist DR test.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 6 > Security Test and Assessment > Disaster Recovery Test Types and Considerations

questions.question: Which TWO are valid sources of measurement data for a security assessment? (Select TWO.)

options.label: A
options.text: The CEO's favorite color

options.label: B
options.text: Risk assessment/analysis results

options.label: C
options.text: The cafeteria menu

options.label: D
options.text: Vulnerability assessment outcomes categorized by severity

explanation.why_correct: Risk assessment results and severity-categorized vulnerability outcomes (plus incident/recovery timelines) are valid measurement-data sources.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Personal color preference is not assessment data.
why_others_are_wrong.C: The cafeteria menu is irrelevant.

questions.exam_reasoning: Identifies legitimate measurement-data sources.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 6 > Security Test and Assessment > Sources of Measurement Data

options.label: A
options.text: Only the source code of every application

options.label: B
options.text: The office Wi-Fi password

options.label: C
options.text: Compliance status and the perceived risk impact

options.label: D
options.text: A list of employee salaries

explanation.why_correct: Audit reports communicate compliance status against governance/regulations and the perceived risk impact of findings.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Audits report on controls/compliance, not full source code.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Salaries are not audit-report content.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Publishing the Wi-Fi password would be a security risk, not audit content.

questions.question: A critical FIRST step when building a security test and assessment strategy is to:

options.label: A
options.text: Delete all existing logs

options.label: B
options.text: Immediately exploit production systems

options.label: C
options.text: Disable monitoring to reduce noise

options.label: D
options.text: Define the scope of what will be assessed

explanation.why_correct: Defining the scope establishes what systems, controls, and objectives the assessment covers, guiding all subsequent activities.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Exploiting production without scope/authorization is reckless and unauthorized.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Deleting logs destroys evidence and accountability.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Disabling monitoring reduces visibility during assessment.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests scoping as a foundational assessment step.

questions.question: A simulation DR test is BEST described as:

options.label: A
options.text: A scan of all open TCP ports

options.label: B
options.text: A structured walkthrough applied to a specific disaster scenario, evaluating results and corrective actions

options.label: C
options.text: A static analysis of application source code

options.label: D
options.text: A complete production cutover to the cloud

explanation.why_correct: A simulation test applies a structured walkthrough to a specific scenario (e.g., natural or man-made disaster), then evaluates results and corrective actions—without full production impact.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Full production cutover is a full interruption test.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Static source-code analysis is SAST, not a DR test.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Port scanning is a vulnerability-assessment activity.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of the simulation DR test.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 6 > Security Test and Assessment > Disaster Recovery Test Types and Considerations

questions.question: During an assessment, an auditor finds several active accounts belonging to employees who left months ago. This finding MOST directly indicates a weakness in:

options.label: A
options.text: The account deprovisioning/auditing part of the account management lifecycle

options.label: B
options.text: The data center cooling system

options.label: C
options.text: The fire suppression system

options.label: D
options.text: The wireless encryption protocol

explanation.why_correct: Lingering accounts for departed staff indicate failures in account auditing/deprovisioning within the account management lifecycle—an access risk.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Cooling is an environmental control, unrelated to orphaned accounts.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Wireless encryption does not govern account removal.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Fire suppression is a physical safety control.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps orphaned accounts to account-lifecycle/deprovisioning weakness.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 6 > Security Test and Assessment > Account Management Lifecycle

questions.question: The PRIMARY purpose of a vulnerability assessment is to:

options.label: A
options.text: Identify and categorize weaknesses so they can be prioritized and remediated

options.label: B
options.text: Exploit weaknesses to gain full control of systems

options.label: C
options.text: Encrypt all data on the network

options.label: D
options.text: Permanently eliminate all risk

explanation.why_correct: A vulnerability assessment identifies and categorizes weaknesses (often by severity) to reduce risk exposure—it does not exploit them (that is penetration testing).

why_others_are_wrong.B: Exploiting weaknesses is penetration testing, not a vulnerability assessment.
why_others_are_wrong.D: No assessment eliminates all risk.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Assessment finds weaknesses; it does not perform encryption.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes vulnerability assessment (find/categorize) from pen testing (exploit).

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 6 > Conduct Security Testing > Vulnerability Assessments

questions.question: Management wants to know which weaknesses exist on its servers but does NOT want testers to actually break in or disrupt operations. Which activity fits BEST?

options.label: A
options.text: A breach and attack simulation against production

options.label: B
options.text: A full interruption DR test

options.label: C
options.text: A vulnerability assessment/scan

options.label: D
options.text: A full-scope penetration test with exploitation

explanation.why_correct: A vulnerability assessment/scan identifies and reports weaknesses without exploiting them, matching the requirement to avoid intrusion/disruption.

why_others_are_wrong.D: A penetration test actively exploits weaknesses, which management excluded.
why_others_are_wrong.B: A full interruption test disrupts production—out of scope here.
why_others_are_wrong.A: BAS exercises attack techniques, which may be more intrusive than wanted.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps non-intrusive weakness identification to a vulnerability assessment.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 6 > Conduct Security Testing > Vulnerability Assessments

questions.question: The MITRE CVE list and the National Vulnerability Database (NVD) primarily provide:

options.label: A
options.text: Standardized identifiers and details for publicly known vulnerabilities

options.label: B
options.text: Physical access badges for the data center

options.label: C
options.text: Encryption keys for production systems

options.label: D
options.text: A backup power supply for scanners

explanation.why_correct: CVE provides unique identifiers for publicly known vulnerabilities, and the NVD enriches them with details/scoring—both are key vulnerability information sources.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Backup power is a UPS/generator function.
why_others_are_wrong.C: CVE/NVD do not provide encryption keys.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Badges are physical access controls.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps known-vulnerability identifiers to CVE/NVD.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 6 > Conduct Security Testing > Sources for Vulnerability Information

questions.question: The Security Content Automation Protocol (SCAP), created by NIST, primarily exists to:

options.label: A
options.text: Provide backup power to scanners

options.label: B
options.text: Replace the need for any vulnerability scanning

options.label: C
options.text: Encrypt wireless traffic

options.label: D
options.text: Standardize how vulnerability and configuration information is expressed and reported

explanation.why_correct: SCAP standardizes the format/exchange of security content (vulnerabilities, configuration checks, scoring) so tools interoperate and reporting is consistent.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Backup power is unrelated to SCAP.
why_others_are_wrong.B: SCAP standardizes scanning content; it does not replace scanning.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Wireless encryption is WPA2/WPA3, not SCAP.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the standardization purpose of SCAP.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 6 > Conduct Security Testing > Security Content Automation Protocol (SCAP)

questions.question: Within SCAP, the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) is used to:

options.label: A
options.text: Uniquely name a hardware/software platform

options.label: B
options.text: Assign a severity score to a vulnerability to help prioritize remediation

options.label: C
options.text: List the open ports on a host

options.label: D
options.text: Encrypt the scan results

explanation.why_correct: CVSS provides a numeric severity score (e.g., 0–10) for vulnerabilities, helping teams prioritize which to fix first.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Naming a platform is the role of CPE (Common Platform Enumeration).
why_others_are_wrong.C: Listing open ports is a function of a port scan, not CVSS.
why_others_are_wrong.D: CVSS scores severity; it does not encrypt results.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps vulnerability severity scoring to CVSS.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 6 > Conduct Security Testing > SCAP Identification Schemes

questions.question: Common Platform Enumeration (CPE) within SCAP is used to:

options.label: A
options.text: Provide standardized names for hardware, operating systems, and applications

options.label: B
options.text: Score the severity of a vulnerability

options.label: C
options.text: Map a network's physical cabling

options.label: D
options.text: Define interactive checklist questions

explanation.why_correct: CPE is a standardized naming scheme for platforms (hardware, OS, applications), enabling consistent identification across tools.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Severity scoring is CVSS.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Interactive checklist questions are OCIL.
why_others_are_wrong.C: CPE does not map physical cabling.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps platform naming to CPE.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 6 > Conduct Security Testing > SCAP Identification Schemes

questions.question: Which TWO of the following are SCAP components? (Select TWO.)

options.label: A
options.text: SYN flood

options.label: B
options.text: XCCDF

options.label: C
options.text: WPA3

options.label: D
options.text: OVAL

explanation.why_correct: XCCDF (configuration checklists) and OVAL (vulnerability/assessment language) are SCAP components, along with OCIL, CPE, CVE, and CVSS.

why_others_are_wrong.C: WPA3 is a wireless encryption protocol.
why_others_are_wrong.A: A SYN flood is a DoS attack technique.

questions.exam_reasoning: Identifies SCAP components.

questions.question: A team needs to verify exact patch levels and detailed configurations on servers. Which scan type provides this deeper insight, and what does it require?

options.label: A
options.text: A credentialed (authenticated) scan, which requires privileged login access

options.label: B
options.text: A non-credentialed scan, which needs no access at all

options.label: C
options.text: A SYN scan, which only checks port state

options.label: D
options.text: A discovery scan, which only finds live hosts

explanation.why_correct: A credentialed/authenticated scan logs in with privileged access to reveal patch levels and detailed configurations—deeper than a non-credentialed scan.

why_others_are_wrong.B: A non-credentialed scan only checks general settings/communications with limited depth.
why_others_are_wrong.D: A discovery scan finds active hosts, not detailed patch levels.
why_others_are_wrong.C: A SYN scan determines port status, not configuration/patch detail.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps deep patch/config insight to credentialed scans.

questions.question: A non-credentialed vulnerability scan is characterized by:

options.label: A
options.text: Logging in as root to read every configuration file

options.label: B
options.text: Checking general settings/communications with read-only access and limited depth

options.label: C
options.text: Requiring physical access to each server

options.label: D
options.text: Always taking longer than a credentialed scan

explanation.why_correct: A non-credentialed scan inspects externally visible settings/communications with read-only access—faster but shallower than a credentialed scan.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Root login for deep config reading describes a credentialed scan.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Non-credentialed scans are typically faster, not slower.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Scans are network-based; they do not require physical access.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the read-only, limited-depth nature of non-credentialed scans.

questions.question: A discovery scan is primarily used to:

options.label: A
options.text: Encrypt host communications

options.text: Score vulnerabilities with CVSS

options.label: C
options.text: Exploit a vulnerability to gain shell access

options.label: D
options.text: Detect active hosts across an IP range/subnet to maintain an inventory

questions.question: In scan results, a port reported as "filtered" generally means:

options.label: A
options.text: The port is definitely open and accepting connections

options.label: B
options.text: A firewall or filter is blocking the scanner from determining the port's true state

options.label: C
options.text: The port is physically disconnected

options.label: D
options.text: The host does not exist

explanation.why_correct: A filtered (unknown/filtered) result indicates a firewall/filter is preventing the scanner from confirming whether the port is open or closed.

why_others_are_wrong.A: An open port would be reported as "open," not filtered.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Filtering is a logical block, not a physical disconnection.

questions.question: An XMAS scan sends packets with which characteristic to probe a target's response?

options.label: A
options.text: A completed three-way handshake on every port

options.label: B
options.text: Multiple TCP flags set (e.g., FIN, PSH, URG) "lighting up" the packet

options.label: C
options.text: No flags and an empty payload only

options.label: D
options.text: Only the SYN flag set

explanation.why_correct: An XMAS scan sets several TCP flags (commonly FIN, PSH, URG) at once—"lit up like a Christmas tree"—to elicit responses that reveal port state while sometimes evading basic logging.

why_others_are_wrong.A: A completed handshake on every port describes a TCP Connect scan.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Only the SYN flag set describes a SYN scan.
why_others_are_wrong.C: A no-flags packet describes a NULL scan, not XMAS.

questions.exam_reasoning: Identifies the multi-flag XMAS scan.

questions.question: A SYN (half-open) scan is often preferred over a full TCP Connect scan because it:

options.label: A
options.text: Always completes the full handshake and logs every connection

options.label: B
options.text: Does not complete the three-way handshake, making it stealthier and faster

options.label: C
options.text: Encrypts the scan traffic end to end

options.label: D
options.text: Requires privileged credentials on the target

explanation.why_correct: A SYN scan sends SYN and interprets the response without completing the handshake (sending RST instead of ACK), making it faster and less likely to be fully logged than a TCP Connect scan.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Completing the handshake/logging describes a TCP Connect scan.
why_others_are_wrong.D: A SYN scan does not require target credentials.
why_others_are_wrong.C: A SYN scan does not encrypt its traffic.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests why SYN (half-open) scans are stealthier than TCP Connect scans.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 6 > Conduct Security Testing > Types of Packet Scans in Vulnerability Scanning

questions.question: A TCP Connect scan differs from a SYN scan in that it:

options.label: A
options.text: Requires the XMAS flag combination

options.label: B
options.text: Never receives any response from the target

options.label: C
options.text: Can only scan UDP services

options.label: D
options.text: Completes the full three-way handshake, which is more easily logged

explanation.why_correct: A TCP Connect scan fully establishes the connection (completes the handshake), which is reliable but more likely to be logged than a half-open SYN scan.

why_others_are_wrong.B: It does receive handshake responses; that is how it confirms open ports.
why_others_are_wrong.C: TCP Connect scans target TCP services, not only UDP.
why_others_are_wrong.A: XMAS is a different scan technique.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes the full-handshake TCP Connect scan from SYN.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 6 > Conduct Security Testing > Types of Packet Scans in Vulnerability Scanning

questions.question: A vulnerability scanning best practice is to:

options.label: A

explanation.why_correct: Scanners must be kept updated (new signatures/plugins) and scans planned/scheduled (e.g., incremental scanning) to remain effective against current threats.

why_others_are_wrong.A: One-time scanning misses newly disclosed vulnerabilities.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Scans should be scheduled thoughtfully, not permanently disabled.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Outdated scanners miss new vulnerabilities; updates are essential.

questions.question: A signature-based vulnerability scanner detects issues by:

options.label: B
options.text: Encrypting files to test resilience

options.label: C
options.text: Randomly guessing passwords until one works

options.label: D
options.text: Physically inspecting cabling

explanation.why_correct: Signature-based scanners match observed system attributes against a database of known vulnerability signatures—so the signature database must stay current.

why_others_are_wrong.C: Password guessing is a brute-force attack, not signature scanning.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Encrypting files is not how scanners detect vulnerabilities.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Cabling inspection is a physical activity, not a scan.

questions.question: A vulnerability scan against a fragile legacy system causes it to crash. Which practice would BEST reduce this risk in the future?

questions.question: UDP scans are often slower and less reliable than TCP scans because UDP:

options.label: A

options.label: D

explanation.why_correct: UDP is connectionless—no handshake—so a lack of response is ambiguous (open|filtered), making UDP scans slower and harder to interpret.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 6 > Conduct Security Testing > Penetration Testing Phases

questions.question: The discovery (reconnaissance) phase of a penetration test focuses on:

options.label: A
options.text: Writing the executive summary

options.label: B
options.text: Moving laterally across compromised systems

options.label: C
options.text: Exploiting vulnerabilities with Metasploit

options.label: D
options.text: Passive information gathering (OSINT/footprinting) without interacting with the target

explanation.why_correct: The discovery phase uses passive reconnaissance—OSINT and footprinting—to gather information without touching the target.

why_others_are_wrong.C: Exploitation occurs in a later phase.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Lateral movement is part of post-exploitation.
why_others_are_wrong.A: The executive summary belongs to the reporting phase.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps passive OSINT/footprinting to the discovery phase.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 6 > Conduct Security Testing > Penetration Testing Phases

questions.question: The scanning phase of a penetration test involves:

options.label: A
options.text: Passive OSINT only, with no system interaction

options.label: B
options.text: Covering tracks by deleting log files

options.label: C
options.text: Negotiating the rules of engagement

options.label: D
options.text: Active reconnaissance such as ping sweeps, port scans, and banner grabbing

explanation.why_correct: The scanning (active reconnaissance) phase interacts with the target—ping sweeps, port scans, banner grabbing, vulnerability scans—to identify weaknesses.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Passive-only OSINT is the discovery phase.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Covering tracks occurs in post-exploitation.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Rules of engagement are agreed before testing begins.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps active recon (scanning) to the scanning phase.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 6 > Conduct Security Testing > Penetration Testing Phases

questions.question: After gaining a foothold on one server, a tester pivots to other systems, maintains access, and removes evidence of activity. Which phase does this represent?

options.label: A
options.text: Post-exploitation

options.label: B
options.text: Scanning

options.label: C
options.text: Discovery

options.label: D
options.text: Reporting

explanation.why_correct: Post-exploitation uses initial access to move laterally, maintain access/persistence, and cover tracks (evading detection).

why_others_are_wrong.C: Discovery is passive pre-attack information gathering.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Scanning is active reconnaissance before exploitation.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Reporting documents findings after testing.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps lateral movement/persistence/track-covering to post-exploitation.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 6 > Conduct Security Testing > Penetration Testing Phases

questions.question: The reporting phase of a penetration test should include:

options.label: A
options.text: No documentation, to keep results secret from the client

options.label: B
options.text: Live exploit code released publicly before remediation

options.label: C
options.text: An executive summary and a technical report, mapping findings to the rules of engagement

options.label: D
options.text: Only a single CVSS number with no context

explanation.why_correct: The reporting phase documents findings, vulnerabilities, and remediation for different audiences (executive summary + technical report), mapping results to the rules of engagement.

why_others_are_wrong.D: A bare score without context does not help remediation.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Releasing exploits publicly before fixes is reckless and unethical.
why_others_are_wrong.A: The client must receive documented findings—that is the deliverable.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests appropriate pen-test reporting content.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 6 > Conduct Security Testing > Penetration Testing Phases

questions.question: After completing an authorized penetration test, the team should perform post-test cleanup, which means:

options.label: A
options.text: Permanently deleting the client's production data

options.label: B
options.text: Leaving backdoors in place for future tests

options.label: C
options.text: Recovering affected hosts, removing tools/scripts, and restoring systems to their original state

options.label: D
options.text: Publishing the client's vulnerabilities online

explanation.why_correct: Post-test cleanup restores systems to their original state—recovering hosts and removing any tools, scripts, or artifacts introduced during testing.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Leaving backdoors is unethical and dangerous.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Deleting production data is destructive and out of scope.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Publishing client vulnerabilities violates confidentiality and ethics.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the restore-to-original-state goal of post-test cleanup.

questions.question: Penetration testing can target which of the following?

options.label: A

options.text: Only printed documents

options.label: C
options.text: Both logical controls (networks/software) and physical controls (locks/cameras)

options.text: Only the HVAC system

explanation.why_correct: Pen tests can assess both logical controls (network/software systems) and physical controls (locks, cameras), depending on scope.

why_others_are_wrong.B: They are not limited to printed documents.
why_others_are_wrong.D: They are not limited to HVAC.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the logical-and-physical scope of pen testing.

questions.question: During an incident investigation, logs from different servers show inconsistent timestamps, making it hard to correlate events. Which control would have PREVENTED this problem?

options.label: A
options.text: Storing logs only on the compromised host

options.label: B
options.text: Disabling logging on half the servers

options.label: C
options.text: Synchronizing all systems to a common time source via NTP

options.label: D
options.text: Using a different time zone per server with no reference

explanation.why_correct: Synchronizing clocks via NTP ensures consistent timestamps across systems, which is essential for correlating events during log review and investigations.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Disabling logging removes the evidence entirely.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Storing logs only on the compromised host risks tampering and loss.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Unreferenced per-server time zones worsen correlation problems.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps timestamp correlation to NTP clock synchronization.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 6 > Conduct Security Testing > Log Reviews

questions.question: To protect log integrity, a recommended practice is to:

options.label: A
options.text: Keep logs only on the originating host with no copies

options.label: B
options.text: Allow all users to edit logs freely

options.label: C
options.text: Delete logs daily to save space

options.label: D
options.text: Store logs on a remote/centralized server and periodically hash them

explanation.why_correct: Storing logs on remote/centralized servers (limiting local tampering) and periodically hashing them to verify integrity are sound log-protection practices.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Local-only logs can be altered or destroyed by an attacker on that host.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Freely editable logs lose integrity.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Deleting logs daily can violate retention policy and destroy evidence.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests remote storage + hashing for log integrity.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 6 > Conduct Security Testing > Log Protection and Security Best Practices

questions.question: The PRIMARY purpose of reviewing system logs is to:

options.label: A
options.text: Track system events and provide an audit trail for detecting/investigating issues

options.label: B
options.text: Increase network bandwidth

options.label: C
options.text: Provide backup power to servers

options.label: D
options.text: Encrypt data at rest automatically

explanation.why_correct: Logs record system events and form audit trails that support detection, investigation, and accountability.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Logs do not increase bandwidth.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Logging is not data-at-rest encryption.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Backup power is a UPS/generator function.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of the audit-trail purpose of logs.

questions.question: In the exploitation phase, testers attempt to:

options.label: C
options.text: Write the final executive summary

options.label: D
options.text: Bypass security controls (manually or with tools like Metasploit) to compromise the target

why_others_are_wrong.B: Gathering public OSINT is the discovery phase.
why_others_are_wrong.C: The executive summary belongs to reporting.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Clock synchronization is a log-review/operations concern.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps active compromise to the exploitation phase.

questions.question: Compared to a periodic manual penetration test, a key advantage of BAS is that it:

options.label: A
options.text: Eliminates the need to ever patch systems

options.label: B
options.text: Requires no security controls to be present

options.label: C
options.text: Provides legal authorization automatically

options.label: D
options.text: Can run continuously/automatically to repeatedly validate control effectiveness

explanation.why_correct: BAS automates simulated attacks so control effectiveness can be validated continuously, complementing point-in-time manual pen tests.

why_others_are_wrong.B: BAS validates existing controls; it does not remove the need for them.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Patching is still required regardless of BAS.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Authorization still comes from rules of engagement, not BAS itself.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the continuous/automated advantage of BAS.

questions.question: Why is documented authorization (in the rules of engagement) essential before testing?

options.label: A
options.text: It provides legal cover so testers are not committing unauthorized access

options.label: B
options.text: It guarantees no vulnerabilities will be found

options.label: C
options.text: It encrypts the network automatically

options.label: D
options.text: It makes the test run faster

explanation.why_correct: Without documented authorization, the same actions a pen tester performs would be illegal unauthorized access; the rules of engagement provide the necessary legal cover.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Authorization is about legality, not speed.
why_others_are_wrong.C: It does not encrypt the network.
why_others_are_wrong.B: It does not affect whether vulnerabilities exist.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the legal-authorization purpose of rules of engagement.

questions.question: Which TWO statements about testing teams are correct? (Select TWO.)

options.label: B
options.text: The blue team writes the marketing plan

options.label: C
options.text: The red team emulates real-world attackers

options.label: D

explanation.why_correct: The red team emulates attackers and the blue team handles detection/defense; together (purple) they improve posture.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Marketing plans are unrelated to the blue team.

questions.question: A board asks why a clean vulnerability scan is not sufficient and why a penetration test was also commissioned. The BEST justification is that a pen test:

options.text: Is cheaper and faster than a scan in every case

options.text: Removes the need to ever scan again

options.label: D
options.text: Demonstrates whether identified weaknesses are actually exploitable and what real impact they have

explanation.why_correct: A scan finds potential weaknesses; a pen test validates which are truly exploitable and demonstrates real business impact, informing prioritization.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Pen tests are usually more involved/costly than scans, not cheaper in every case.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Scanning remains a regular, complementary practice.
why_others_are_wrong.A: No test guarantees an unbreachable network.

questions.question: Unit testing focuses on:

options.label: A
options.text: How the entire integrated system meets all requirements

options.label: B
options.text: How two or more technologies work together

options.label: C
options.text: Individual components, scripts, or features in isolation

options.label: D
options.text: Whether a change broke previously working functionality

explanation.why_correct: Unit testing targets specific applications, scripts, or components in isolation, assessing a feature's security/performance/usability.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Testing the entire system against requirements is system/acceptance testing.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Testing how technologies work together is integration testing.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Checking that changes did not break existing functionality is regression testing.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes unit testing from system/integration/regression.

questions.question: Integration testing verifies:

options.label: A
options.text: The speed of the office network

options.label: B
options.text: How two or more components/technologies work together

options.label: C
options.text: A single isolated function only

options.label: D
options.text: That the entire system meets acceptance criteria

explanation.why_correct: Integration testing checks that combined components/technologies interact correctly.

why_others_are_wrong.C: A single isolated function is unit testing.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Whole-system acceptance is system testing.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Network speed is unrelated to integration testing.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of integration testing.

questions.question: After patching a bug, a team re-runs tests to confirm the fix did not break any previously working features. This is:

options.label: A
options.text: Fuzz testing

options.label: B
options.text: Unit testing

options.label: C
options.text: Regression testing

options.label: D
options.text: Smoke testing

explanation.why_correct: Regression testing ensures recent changes have not adversely affected existing functionality.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Unit testing checks an isolated component, not the impact of a change on the whole.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Smoke testing is a quick basic-functionality check after a build.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Fuzz testing sends invalid input to find flaws.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps "did the change break anything" to regression testing.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 6 > Conduct Security Testing > Types of Software Tests

questions.question: System testing (also called acceptance testing or a reasonableness check) verifies that:

options.label: A
options.text: The software meets its functional and security requirements as a whole

options.label: B
options.text: Invalid inputs cause crashes

options.label: C
options.text: Two modules exchange data

options.label: D
options.text: A single function behaves correctly in isolation

explanation.why_correct: System/acceptance testing validates the complete software against its functional and security requirements.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Isolated single-function testing is unit testing.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Driving crashes via invalid input is fuzz testing.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Module-to-module data exchange is integration testing.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of system/acceptance testing.

questions.question: Smoke testing is BEST described as:

options.label: A

options.label: C
options.text: A review of the disaster recovery plan

options.label: D
options.text: An exhaustive test of every code path

explanation.why_correct: Smoke testing quickly verifies that the core functionality of a build works before deeper testing proceeds.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Exhaustive path testing is coverage-focused, not a quick smoke test.
why_others_are_wrong.B: A perimeter pen test is unrelated to build smoke testing.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Reviewing a DR plan is a checklist DR test.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of smoke testing.

questions.question: Fuzz testing discovers vulnerabilities by:

options.text: Encrypting the application's database

options.text: Sending invalid, unexpected, or random data to an application to see how it responds

explanation.why_correct: Fuzz testing injects invalid/unexpected/random inputs to uncover crashes, vulnerabilities, or performance issues.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Reviewing code without running it is static testing (SAST).
why_others_are_wrong.C: Encrypting a database is unrelated to fuzzing.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Clock synchronization is NTP, not fuzzing.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes mutation fuzzing from generational fuzzing?

options.label: A
options.text: Both are identical and use no input data

options.label: B
options.text: Neither produces invalid inputs

options.label: C
options.text: Mutation fuzzing builds inputs from a model; generational fuzzing alters valid data

options.label: D
options.text: Mutation (dumb) fuzzing alters valid data to create invalid inputs; generational (smart) fuzzing builds inputs from a model

explanation.why_correct: Mutation (dumb) fuzzing modifies existing valid data into invalid inputs; generational (smart) fuzzing synthesizes inputs using a model of the expected format.

why_others_are_wrong.C: This reverses the two techniques.
why_others_are_wrong.A: They differ in how inputs are produced.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Both produce invalid inputs to probe the target.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes mutation (dumb) from generational (smart) fuzzing.

questions.question: A security team wants to find insecure code patterns early by analyzing source code WITHOUT executing the application. Which approach fits BEST?

why_others_are_wrong.A: A parking permit is unrelated.

questions.exam_reasoning: Identifies testable interface types.

questions.question: A SaaS provider wants a report attesting to its SECURITY and privacy controls that it can share (under NDA) with prospective customers' auditors. Which SOC report fits BEST?

options.label: A
options.text: SOC 1

options.label: B
options.text: PCI ROC

options.label: C
options.text: SOC 2

options.label: D
options.text: SOC 3

explanation.why_correct: SOC 2 reports on security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality, and privacy controls—appropriate for detailed sharing with customers/auditors under NDA.

why_others_are_wrong.A: SOC 1 focuses on controls relevant to financial reporting.
why_others_are_wrong.D: SOC 3 is a high-level public summary, lacking the detail auditors need.
why_others_are_wrong.B: A PCI ROC concerns payment-card compliance, not general security-control attestation.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps security/privacy control attestation to SOC 2.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 6 > Conduct Security Testing > Compliance Testing

questions.question: Match each SOC report (1-3) to its focus (A-C).

options.label: A

options.label: B
options.text: Controls relevant to financial reporting

options.label: C
options.text: Security and privacy controls (detailed, for restricted distribution)

explanation.why_correct: SOC 1 → financial-reporting controls (B); SOC 2 → security/privacy controls (A); SOC 3 → high-level public summary (C).

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests mapping of SOC report types to their focus.

questions.question: A SOC 3 report is intended to be:

options.label: C
options.text: A disaster recovery checklist

options.label: D
options.text: A high-level summary suitable for public/general distribution

explanation.why_correct: SOC 3 provides a high-level, general-use summary that can be shared publicly, unlike the detailed SOC 1/SOC 2 reports.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Detailed financial-controls reporting is SOC 1.
why_others_are_wrong.A: A pen test report is a different artifact.
why_others_are_wrong.C: A DR checklist is a continuity document.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of SOC 3 as a public summary.

questions.question: In the CSA STAR program for cloud security, Level 1 versus Level 2 differ in that Level 1 is:

options.label: A
options.text: A financial report, while Level 2 is a privacy report

options.label: B
options.text: A third-party audit, while Level 2 is a self-assessment

options.label: C
options.text: A penetration test, while Level 2 is a vulnerability scan

options.label: D
options.text: A self-assessment, while Level 2 involves a third-party audit

explanation.why_correct: CSA STAR Level 1 is a self-assessment (suited to lower-risk environments); Level 2 involves an independent third-party audit (for higher-risk environments).

why_others_are_wrong.B: This reverses the two levels.
why_others_are_wrong.C: STAR levels are assurance tiers, not pen test vs scan.
why_others_are_wrong.A: STAR is about cloud security assurance, not financial vs privacy reports.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes CSA STAR Level 1 (self) from Level 2 (third-party audit).

questions.question: Compliance testing helps an organization demonstrate:

why_others_are_wrong.C: Compliance requires controls, not their absence.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Marketing effectiveness is unrelated.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Wi-Fi speed is not a compliance outcome.

questions.exam_reasoning: Connects compliance testing to due care/diligence.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Fire safety certificates are physical-safety documents.

questions.question: Branch coverage ensures that:

options.label: A
options.text: Each program function has been called

options.label: B
options.text: Every loop has been exercised

options.label: C
options.text: Every line of code has been executed at least once

options.label: D
options.text: Each decision branch (e.g., both true and false paths) in the code has been tested

explanation.why_correct: Branch coverage verifies that each decision branch (each outcome of a conditional) has been tested.

why_others_are_wrong.C: Executing every line is statement coverage.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Calling each function is function coverage.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Exercising loops is loop coverage.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes branch coverage from statement/function/loop coverage.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 6 > Conduct Security Testing > Branch Coverage

questions.question: Statement coverage measures whether:

options.label: A
options.text: Every loop iteration boundary was tested

options.label: B
options.text: Each decision branch outcome was tested

options.label: C
options.text: Every interface was fuzzed

options.label: D
options.text: Each individual code statement has been executed during testing

explanation.why_correct: Statement coverage tracks whether each executable statement in the code has been run at least once during testing.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Testing each branch outcome is branch coverage.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Loop-boundary testing is loop coverage.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Fuzzing interfaces is a different activity.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of statement coverage.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 6 > Conduct Security Testing > Statement Coverage

questions.question: A test suite exercises 30 of a module's 60 executable statements. The statement coverage and the implied confidence level are:

options.label: A
options.text: 30% coverage

options.label: B
options.text: Cannot be determined from the numbers given

options.label: C
options.text: 200% coverage

options.label: D
options.text: 50% coverage (tested items divided by total items)

explanation.why_correct: Coverage = items tested / total items = 30/60 = 50%; higher coverage generally implies greater confidence in testing.

why_others_are_wrong.C: 200% is impossible; coverage cannot exceed 100%.
why_others_are_wrong.A: 30% would require 18 of 60, not 30 of 60.
why_others_are_wrong.B: The ratio is directly computable from the figures.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the coverage = tested/total calculation.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 6 > Conduct Security Testing > Test Coverage Analysis

questions.question: Loop coverage is important for security/reliability because it helps prevent:

options.label: A
options.text: Service outages caused by improperly terminating (continuous) loops

options.label: B
options.text: Physical tailgating into the building

options.label: C
options.text: Weak wireless encryption

options.label: D
options.text: DNS poisoning

explanation.why_correct: Loop coverage tests loop behavior (including boundaries), helping catch loops that never terminate and could cause outages.

why_others_are_wrong.C: Wireless encryption is unrelated to loop coverage.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Tailgating is a physical-security issue.
why_others_are_wrong.D: DNS poisoning is a network attack, not a loop defect.

questions.exam_reasoning: Connects loop coverage to preventing runaway-loop outages.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 6 > Conduct Security Testing > Loop Coverage

questions.question: Function (functional) coverage ensures that:

options.label: A
options.text: Each program function has been tested/called for verification

options.label: B
options.text: Every statement is executed

options.label: C
options.text: Each decision branch is tested

options.label: D
options.text: Each loop boundary is exercised

explanation.why_correct: Function coverage verifies that each program function has been exercised during testing.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Loop boundaries are loop coverage.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Executing every statement is statement coverage.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Testing each branch is branch coverage.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of function coverage.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 6 > Conduct Security Testing > Functional Coverage (Function Coverage)

questions.question: The executive summary of a test/assessment report is primarily written for:

questions.question: Which statement BEST distinguishes an assessment report from an audit report?

options.label: A

options.text: An assessment report is only for attackers

options.label: C
options.text: An audit report contains no findings at all

options.label: D
options.text: An assessment report conveys security findings/recommendations, while an audit report attests to compliance status against criteria

explanation.why_correct: An assessment report communicates security findings and recommendations; an audit report formally attests to compliance status against defined criteria.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Reports are for stakeholders, not attackers.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Audit reports do contain findings (compliance status/exceptions).

questions.question: Ethical disclosure of test findings primarily ensures:

questions.question: Remediation recommendations in a report typically suggest:

questions.question: The KEY difference between static and dynamic testing is that static testing:

options.text: Runs the code, while dynamic testing only reads it

why_others_are_wrong.D: "Fire-drill testing" is not a software testing knowledge category.

options.text: Only whether each loop ran once

options.text: Only whether each function was called

options.label: D
options.text: Each individual boolean sub-condition within a decision

explanation.why_correct: Condition coverage checks each boolean sub-condition (operand) within a decision, which is finer-grained than branch coverage (which checks decision outcomes).

why_others_are_wrong.C: Function calls are function coverage.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Statement execution is statement coverage.

why_others_are_wrong.C: Omitting findings defeats the report's purpose.
